target.name: mitochondrial DNA replication
target.description: Each mitochondrion carries its own small circular genome encoding respiratory chain subunits and the tRNAs and rRNAs needed to make them, and mitochondrial DNA replication is how that genome is copied and kept at adequate copy number in every tissue. Loss of this capacity produces mtDNA depletion and multiple-deletion syndromes, with hepatocerebral disease, progressive external ophthalmoplegia, myopathy and neuropathy following the tissues that depend most on oxidative phosphorylation.

target.name: renal water absorption
target.description: Concentrating urine depends on renal water absorption, the recovery of water from tubular fluid across the proximal tubule, descending limb and collecting duct back into the blood. It is how the body defends plasma osmolality and blood volume during dehydration, and its failure produces diabetes insipidus, with large volumes of dilute urine and unquenchable thirst.

target.name: Activated NTRK3 signals through PLCG1
target.description: Neurotrophin-3 binding to its receptor tyrosine kinase TRKC recruits and phosphorylates phospholipase C-gamma 1, one of the branches by which this receptor converts a neurotrophic signal into a cellular response. The output matters for neuronal survival, differentiation and synaptic function: NT-3/TRKC signalling supports proprioceptive sensory neurons and cerebellar and hippocampal populations, and its loss produces defects in limb proprioception and movement coordination.

target.name: cyclooxygenase pathway
target.description: Prostaglandins are short-lived lipid mediators that set vascular tone, platelet behaviour, fever, pain sensitivity and the inflammatory response, and the cyclooxygenase pathway is how they are made from arachidonic acid released from membrane phospholipids. The committed step is carried out by prostaglandin-endoperoxide synthase, in constitutive (PTGS1) and inducible (PTGS2) forms, which converts arachidonate to the unstable endoperoxides PGG2 and PGH2; this is the step blocked by aspirin and other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs.
